title: Pseudocode: sequence, selection and iteration
specPoints: Produce and interpret algorithms using **pseudocode** (OCR Exam Reference Language) and a high-level language
learn: Read and write algorithms in OCR Exam Reference Language
Choose the right kind of loop for a problem and explain the choice
Convert a flowchart into pseudocode and pseudocode into a flowchart
hook: Here is a flowchart from last lesson, and here is the same algorithm written in eight lines of text. Which would you rather type into a computer? Which would you rather read on an exam paper? Today you learn to write the text version the way OCR writes it.

video.title: OCR pseudocode in one go: sequence, selection, iteration
video.brief: 5 minutes. Three panels. 1) Sequence: three lines run top to bottom, highlight each. 2) Selection: the password flowchart from lesson 3 morphs into `if … then / else / endif`; show `elseif` for the temperature example. 3) Iteration: `for i = 1 to 10` (count-controlled, we know how many), `while answer != "yes"` (condition first, may run zero times), `do … until` (condition after, runs at least once). Run each with a counter visible. End with the OCR reference card: `input`, `print`, `=`, `==`, `!=`, `MOD`, `DIV`, keywords in lowercase, `endif / endwhile / next i`.

explain.h: Why OCR has its own pseudocode
p: Pseudocode is code written for humans: precise enough to follow, but not tied to one language. OCR publishes an **Exam Reference Language (ERL)** so every question uses the same conventions. In the exam you can answer in ERL **or** real Python; both score. But you must be able to **read** ERL because questions are written in it.
Statements run one after another, top to bottom. Assignment uses `=`; comparison uses `==`. Input and output:
explain.code:
name = input("What is your name?")
age = int(input("Age?"))
print("Hello " + name)
next_year = age + 1

p: A decision chooses which lines run. Every `if` is closed by `endif`. Use `elseif` for a chain of tests and `else` for everything else:
explain.code:
if temp < 0 then
    print("FREEZING")
elseif temp >= 25 then
    print("HOT")
else
    print("MILD")
endif
after: `switch … case` does the same job when you are comparing one variable against fixed values. Comparison operators: `==  !=  <  <=  >  >=`. Boolean operators: `AND  OR  NOT`.

explain.code:
for i = 1 to 10
    print(i)
next i
after: **Condition-controlled, condition first** — may run zero times:
**Condition-controlled, condition last** — always runs at least once:
Choosing the right loop is a frequent exam mark: *do you know how many times?* → `for`. *Might it not need to run at all?* → `while`. *Must it run at least once?* → `do…until`.

p: Each process box is one line. Each decision becomes `if … then … else … endif`. A decision whose No arrow goes back is a `while` (if the test is before the body) or `do…until` (if the test is after). Indent the body of every `if` and loop; OCR marks are easier to get when the structure is visible.
Pseudocode is code you write for people to read. OCR has its own version so every exam question looks the same. You can answer in it or in Python.

simple.code:
name = input("What is your name?")
print("Hello " + name)

p: `if` asks a question. `then` runs when the answer is yes. `else` runs when it is no. `endif` closes it.
simple.code:
if temp < 0 then
    print("FREEZING")
else
    print("OK")
endif

p: `for` when you know how many times. `while` when you keep going as long as something is true (checks first). `do … until` when you keep going until something is true (checks after, so it always runs once).
simple.code:
for i = 1 to 10
    print(i)
next i

while answer != "yes"
    answer = input("Finished?")
endwhile

do
    password = input("Password?")
until password == "letmein"

keyterms.def: A way of writing an algorithm in structured English-like code that is not tied to one programming language.
Instructions executed one after another in order.
Choosing which instructions to run based on a condition (if, elseif, else, switch).
Repeating instructions: count-controlled (for) or condition-controlled (while, do…until).
An expression that is either true or false, e.g. `age >= 18`.

try.title: 1. Run OCR pseudocode for real
instructions: Type the temperature `if / elseif / else` program from above. Run it with −3, 10 and 30.
Change `>= 25` to `> 25`. Run it with 25. What changed and why?
Write a `for` loop that prints the 7 times table from 1 × 7 to 12 × 7.

try.title: 2. Choose the loop
p: For each situation, say which loop fits (`for`, `while` or `do…until`) and write it in ERL:
steps: Keep asking for a number until the user types a number between 1 and 10.
While there are still items in a shopping list, take the next one off and print it (the list might be empty to start with).

try.title: 3. Flowchart to pseudocode
p: Convert the password flowchart from lesson 3 (ask, check, loop back until "letmein", output "Access granted") into pseudocode. Use the loop that fits best, and say in one sentence why you chose it.

try.title: 4. Parsons puzzle: put the lines in order
instructions: Open a puzzle and drag the shuffled lines into a working program. Indentation matters — it shows what is inside the loop or the if.

check.q: Which operator **compares** two values in OCR pseudocode?
A loop that must run at least once and stops when a condition becomes true is:
Which keyword closes an `if` in ERL?
You need to print each name in a list of exactly 30 names. Best loop?
`while x > 10` with x starting at 5. How many times does the body run?
check.fb: The condition is false at the start, so a `while` loop never runs.

exam.q: Write an algorithm in pseudocode that asks the user to enter a mark out of 100 and outputs "Pass" if the mark is 40 or more, otherwise "Fail".
model: `mark = int(input("Enter mark"))` (1 — input stored in a variable)
exam.commentary: The boundary (`>=` not `>`) is a deliberate mark. Students writing `mark > 39` are fine. Missing `endif` is not usually penalised on its own, but missing the `else` output is. Python is accepted; be consistent — don't mix `then` with Python colons.

exam.q: The following algorithm is written in OCR pseudocode. State the output.
exam.code:
total = 0
for i = 1 to 4
    total = total + i * 2
next i
print(total)
exam.commentary: Full marks for 20. If wrong, one mark is available for working that shows the loop runs 4 times with 2, 4, 6, 8 added. Students who stop at i = 3 (12) have misread `to 4` as 'less than 4' — in ERL `for i = 1 to 4` is inclusive.

exam.q: Explain why a `while` loop rather than a `for` loop is used to repeatedly ask a user for a valid password.
model: The number of attempts is not known in advance (1), so the loop must continue until a condition (correct password) is met rather than a fixed number of times (1).
exam.commentary: Both halves needed: *unknown count* and *stops on a condition*. 'Because it's better' earns nothing.

home: Write three short programs in ERL: (1) a for loop that prints the even numbers from 2 to 20; (2) a do…until loop that asks for a PIN until it is 1234; (3) an if/elseif/else that converts a mark to a grade (≥70 A, ≥50 B, else C). Test them in the pseudocode runner.

teacher.timing: 60 min: hook 4 · explain 15 · try 25 · check 5 · exam 8 · homework 3
misconceptions: `=` vs `==`. Drill it: 'single equals puts a value in; double equals asks a question'.
`for i = 1 to 4` treated as exclusive of 4 (Python's `range` habit). ERL is inclusive.
Choosing `for` for everything. Keep asking 'do you know how many times?'
Forgetting that `while` can run zero times and `do…until` cannot.
say: 'Read the condition out loud with the word *while* in front: while answer is not yes… keep asking.'
'Indent means inside. If it isn't indented, it isn't in the loop.'
teacher.skip: Try 4 (Parsons) can be set as homework. Prioritise Try 1 in the pseudocode runner — seeing ERL run is what makes it stick.
differentiation: Support: give the three loop templates on a card; students fill in the condition and body only.
Stretch: rewrite the do…until as a while loop and explain what changed (needs a first input before the loop).

pt.title: Pseudocódigo: sequência, seleção e iteração
pt.hook: Aqui está um fluxograma da aula passada e aqui o mesmo algoritmo em oito linhas de texto. Qual preferias escrever no computador? Qual preferias ler num exame? Hoje aprendes a escrever a versão em texto como a OCR a escreve.

explain.h: Porque é que a OCR tem o seu próprio pseudocódigo
p: Pseudocódigo é código escrito para pessoas: suficientemente preciso para ser seguido, mas sem estar ligado a uma linguagem. A OCR publica uma **Exam Reference Language (ERL)** para que todas as perguntas usem as mesmas convenções. No exame podes responder em ERL **ou** em Python; ambos contam. Mas tens de saber **ler** ERL, porque as perguntas são escritas nela.
As instruções correm uma após outra, de cima para baixo. Atribuição usa `=`; comparação usa `==`. Entrada e saída:
explain.code:
name = input("What is your name?")
age = int(input("Age?"))
print("Hello " + name)
next_year = age + 1

p: Uma decisão escolhe que linhas correm. Todo o `if` fecha com `endif`. Usa `elseif` para uma cadeia de testes e `else` para o resto:
explain.code:
if temp < 0 then
    print("FREEZING")
elseif temp >= 25 then
    print("HOT")
else
    print("MILD")
endif
after: Operadores de comparação: `==  !=  <  <=  >  >=`. Operadores lógicos: `AND  OR  NOT`.

p: **Controlado por contagem** — sabes quantas vezes: `for i = 1 to 10 … next i`.
**Controlado por condição, teste primeiro** — pode correr zero vezes: `while condição … endwhile`.
**Controlado por condição, teste no fim** — corre sempre pelo menos uma vez: `do … until condição`.
explain.code:
for i = 1 to 10
    print(i)
next i

while answer != "yes"
    answer = input("Finished?")
endwhile

do
    password = input("Password?")
until password == "letmein"
after: Escolher o ciclo certo vale marcas no exame: *sabes quantas vezes?* → `for`. *Pode não precisar de correr?* → `while`. *Tem de correr pelo menos uma vez?* → `do…until`.

p: Cada caixa de processo é uma linha. Cada decisão passa a `if … then … else … endif`. Uma decisão cuja seta No volta atrás é um `while` (se o teste está antes do corpo) ou `do…until` (se está depois). Indenta o corpo de cada `if` e de cada ciclo.

keyterms.def: Forma de escrever um algoritmo em código estruturado, parecido com inglês, sem estar ligado a uma linguagem.
Instruções executadas uma após outra, por ordem.
Escolher que instruções correm com base numa condição (if, elseif, else, switch).
Repetir instruções: por contagem (for) ou por condição (while, do…until).
Uma expressão que é verdadeira ou falsa, p. ex. `age >= 18`.
